item.title: ETH whales keep buying through the slide while bitcoin whales send coins to exchanges
item.description:
If the split in whale behaviour persists, ETH could hold up better than bitcoin, and that would show first in the ETH/BTC ratio. Buying through trading desks doesn’t show up in spot ETF data, so it can run alongside weak fund flows: US spot bitcoin ETFs lost roughly $2.1 billion between late October and mid-November. Continued net deposits by bitcoin whales leave BTC rallies exposed to fresh supply, a headwind for crypto equities such as COIN and listed miners, which tend to follow the bitcoin price. For wider risk sentiment, steady ETH buying at around $1,765 suggests some large buyers see value after the drop.

-- Ethereum’s big buyers are holding and bitcoin’s big holders are moving coins to sell, a split that is small in dollar terms but worth watching as the market looks for a floor.

Summary:

  • Four wallets withdrew about 13,400 ETH, worth around $23.7 million, from FalconX, Galaxy Digital and OKX
  • Two of them are fresh wallets that have only received ETH from trading desks and now hold about 17,900 ETH combined, with none sold or staked
  • The other two are older trading accounts that each took in about 1,140 ETH after moving USDT, which fits a swap from stablecoins into ETH
  • Bitcoin holders of 1,000 BTC or more are sending roughly $55 million more to exchanges each day than they withdraw
  • Long-dormant bitcoin whales booked around $295 million in profits on 10 November, their biggest profit-taking day of 2026

A cluster of large Ethereum wallets has been quietly adding to holdings through November’s sell-off, offering a contrast with bitcoin, where the biggest holders are still moving coins onto exchanges.

On-chain tracker Lookonchain flagged this week that four wallets withdrew about 13,400 ETH, worth around $23.7 million, from FalconX, Galaxy Digital and OKX, the first two being trading desks that mainly serve institutions. On-chain data, which records every transfer on the blockchain, gives a clearer picture of who received the coins.

Most of the ETH went to two wallets that look like long-term buyers. The larger received about 8,825 ETH in a single transfer from a wallet labelled as FalconX and now holds around 9,430 ETH, roughly $16.7 million. The second, created in mid-August, has taken delivery of between roughly 400 and 1,200 ETH every week or two since then, including through the October and November slide, and now holds about 8,480 ETH. Neither wallet has sold any of its ETH, and neither has staked it, meaning locked it up to help secure the network in return for a yield. Together they hold around 17,900 ETH, worth about $31.6 million at an ETH price of around $1,765.

A new wallet that only ever receives coins from a trading desk usually points to a buyer collecting purchases made off-exchange, often in instalments. The other two wallets are older, actively traded accounts that each received about 1,140 ETH from the same unlabelled sender and had moved USDT, a dollar-pegged stablecoin, shortly before. That fits traders swapping stablecoins into ETH, although the data does not confirm it.

Bitcoin is showing the opposite pattern. Entities holding 1,000 BTC or more are sending roughly $55 million more to exchanges each day than they withdraw, and coins are usually moved onto an exchange to be sold. Long-dormant bitcoin whales also booked around $295 million in profits on 10 November, their biggest profit-taking day of the year.

The ETH buying is modest in size and the owners are unknown, so it is evidence of steady demand from a few large buyers rather than a market-wide shift. The next thing to watch is whether these wallets keep receiving deliveries and whether more fresh, desk-funded wallets appear. Staking deposits from them would signal a longer holding horizon, while transfers back to an exchange would weaken the accumulation case.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NYT: Trump weighs new Iran strikes as Israel presses for a four- to seven-day air campaign
item.description:
A renewed US-Israeli air campaign would raise the risk of Iranian retaliation against Gulf shipping and energy infrastructure. With a loaded tanker already hit in the Strait of Hormuz, traders are likely to keep a larger risk premium in crude until Washington’s intentions are clearer. Higher oil feeds straight into the inflation worries that Fed officials raised this week, adding to the case for further US rate hikes. That’s why gold has tended to weaken rather than rally on escalation in this conflict. Oil importers’ currencies, notably the yen, are vulnerable to a further rise in energy costs. Energy stocks stand to benefit.

---

Israel wants a short, sharp campaign against Iran and Trump hasn’t ruled it out. With a divided administration and voters weary of the war, the decision is finely balanced, and oil is pricing the risk.

Summary:

  • Trump is weighing another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, but has not made a decision
  • Israel is pressing the US to join a four- to seven-day air campaign, citing Iran rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals
  • Israeli officials also warn Iran is advancing its chemical and biological weapons programmes
  • Mossad’s director met the CIA director in Washington last week as talks intensified
  • The administration is divided over the intelligence and the wisdom of new strikes after a midterm backlash against the war
  • Oil rose on the report, with a tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz adding to supply worries

President Donald Trump is weighing another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, as Israel presses Washington to join a four- to seven-day air campaign, according to a New York Times (gated) report citing US and Israeli officials briefed on the discussions. No decision has been made, the officials said, but the report helps explain why oil prices have moved higher on Thursday.

The deliberations are being driven by new intelligence. Israeli officials have warned that Iran has succeeded in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and is advancing chemical and biological weapons programmes. Trump is also said to be weighing the fact that the United States currently has significant military firepower in the region, a window that may not stay open indefinitely.

Talks have intensified over the past week. Mossad director Roman Gofman held meetings in Washington, including with CIA director John Ratcliffe, while other senior Israeli officials, among them military intelligence chief Shlomi Binder, have argued for a resumption of operations in discussions with American counterparts. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose position is described as particularly fragile after elections last month, is pushing hard for joint action.

The administration is far from united. Officials are divided over how strong the intelligence is and whether striking Iran again is wise, particularly after midterm elections in which voters signalled clear unhappiness with a war that has pushed up prices and has not delivered the swift victory promised at its outset nearly eight months ago. That political cost is a meaningful constraint on any decision to escalate.

For markets, the report adds a fresh layer of risk to an oil market that was already on edge. A loaded tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, a reminder that shipping through the world’s most important oil chokepoint remains vulnerable. Reports of possible US military action against Iran have triggered sharp rallies in crude several times this year, and traders are likely to stay sensitive to any signal from the White House in the days ahead.

The key questions now are whether Trump decides to act, how long any campaign would last and whether Iran responds by targeting shipping or regional energy infrastructure. Until there is clarity, the threat of renewed strikes is likely to keep a risk premium built into oil prices. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Musk says Anthropic wants another 10 gigawatts of SpaceX compute, over 30 times its deal Alt headlines:
item.description:
For SpaceX shares, the comments add weight to the AI cloud story, though investors may discount a figure that comes from Musk rather than Anthropic. For the wider AI trade, a demand signal of this size supports chipmakers and power-related names after a punishing week, particularly Nvidia, whose GPUs fill Colossus. Power is the limit. Any real 10 GW build-out would need grid capacity on a scale few regions can offer, which keeps utilities and energy infrastructure in focus. For ANT, the comment is supportive background going into its first day of trading, but early price action is more likely to be driven by IPO demand than by second-hand remarks.

---

Coming up:

  • Anthropic confirms $83 IPO price on 980 million shares in an $81 billion deal

---

If Musk’s account is right, Anthropic wants to rent 30 times more computing power from a company owned by its rival. That’s a striking sign of AI demand, but it’s unconfirmed, comes from an interested party, and power supply is the real constraint.

Summary:

  • Musk said Anthropic is extremely likely to continue renting compute from SpaceX and most likely wants an additional 10 gigawatts
  • Anthropic hasn’t publicly confirmed the figure
  • The current deal covers all of SpaceX’s Colossus 1 data centre, over 300 megawatts and more than 220,000 Nvidia GPUs
  • SpaceX’s IPO filing showed Anthropic paying about $1.25 billion a month over three years for that capacity
  • SpaceX owns xAI, an Anthropic rival, and Musk has been a vocal critic of Anthropic
  • The comments came at the DealBook Summit, the day before Anthropic’s Nasdaq listing

Elon Musk says Anthropic has told SpaceX it is extremely likely to keep renting computing capacity from the company and that its most likely scenario involves an additional 10 gigawatts of compute. Musk, who runs SpaceX as well as Tesla, made the comments at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, on the eve of Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut. Anthropic has not publicly confirmed the figure.

The number is striking against the size of the existing relationship. In May, Anthropic agreed to take all of the computing capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 1 data centre in Memphis, more than 300 megawatts powered by over 220,000 Nvidia chips. SpaceX’s own IPO filing later showed Anthropic paying around $1.25 billion a month for that capacity over three years, roughly $15 billion a year. An extra 10 gigawatts would be more than 30 times the size of the current deal.

The relationship is an unusual one. SpaceX merged with Musk’s AI company xAI earlier this year, making it a direct competitor to Anthropic, and Musk has been a vocal public critic of the Claude developer. Yet the arrangement suits both sides: Anthropic needs vast amounts of computing power to keep up with demand, and SpaceX is positioning itself as an AI cloud landlord, with Musk having previously said Google also rents capacity from the company.

The comments need careful handling. They are Musk’s account of what a customer told him, not a signed contract, and he has an obvious interest in talking up demand for SpaceX’s data centres. A desired 10 gigawatts only becomes revenue once it is financed, powered and built, and power supply is one of the tightest constraints facing the industry.

Even so, the remarks land at a pointed moment. Investors have spent the week questioning whether AI spending can keep growing at its current pace, with chip stocks under pressure and Nvidia at a 16-month low. A demand signal of this size from one of the largest buyers of computing power cuts against that worry, though markets are likely to want confirmation from Anthropic itself before treating it as firm. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia chair tells staff there is no Jensen clone, as leaders pledge strategy continuity
item.description:
On its own, a staff meeting is unlikely to move Nvidia shares much, but the chair’s comments shift the succession story. Investors hoping for a quick handover to a Huang-like figure may now expect a longer search and a different kind of leader. That could keep a governance discount on the stock while the board investigation and the reported SEC probe run their course. The commitment to the Hugging Face deal and open models matters for the wider AI ecosystem, signalling that Nvidia’s push into software isn’t being shelved. With the shares at a 16-month low, investors want hard answers, not reassurance.

--- Nvidia’s first staff meeting after Huang’s exit was mostly a rallying cry, but two lines stood out: the chair admitting Huang can’t be replicated, and a co-founder saying the company’s first value had been violated.

Summary:

  • Nvidia held its first all-hands staff meeting since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO
  • Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company’s ambition won’t change, and executives said the chip roadmap is on track
  • Board chair Harvey Jones said it is unrealistic to expect to find a Jensen clone, calling Huang one of a kind
  • Co-founder Chris Malachowsky became emotional and said a violation of Nvidia’s first core value, maintaining the highest standards, had given him pause
  • Executives said the roughly $13 billion Hugging Face acquisition and the open-model strategy will continue

Nvidia’s leadership used the company’s first all-hands staff meeting since Jensen Huang’s resignation to steady nerves, telling employees the strategy and product roadmap remain intact while conceding that the next chief executive will not be a copy of the founder, according to accounts of the meeting reported on Wednesday.

Interim chief executive Colette Kress set the tone, telling staff the company’s ambition will not change and that they are equipped to handle the moment. Senior executive Ian Buck offered similar reassurance on the chip roadmap, saying the company knows how to deliver it. An introductory video leaned on Nvidia’s history of perseverance and tenacity.

The more revealing remarks came from the board and the company’s founding generation. Board chair Harvey Jones said it was unrealistic to expect the search to produce “a Jensen clone,” describing Huang as one of a kind. That is a notable admission for investors. It suggests the board is prepared to look for a different style of leader rather than a near replica, and it lowers expectations for a quick, seamless succession at a company whose identity has been tightly bound to one person for 33 years.

Co-founder Chris Malachowsky was reported to have become emotional while discussing Nvidia’s first core value, maintaining the highest standards, saying it was the breach of that principle that had given him pause over the past week. Coming from a co-founder, the comment acknowledges that the circumstances of Huang’s departure go to the heart of the company’s culture, not just its org chart.

On strategy, engineering executive Dwight Diercks said the roughly $13 billion acquisition of Hugging Face and the wider push into open AI models will continue, with the goal of making Nvidia the leader in open models. That matters because the open-model strategy extends Nvidia’s reach beyond selling chips into the software ecosystem that keeps developers tied to its hardware.

Pep talks are part of any leadership transition, and the meeting’s message of continuity should be read as what management wants staff and the market to hear. The tests that matter lie elsewhere: the outcome of the board’s independent investigation, a reported Securities and Exchange Commission probe, the choice of a permanent CEO and whether customers and partners keep their commitments. Strong quarterly results this week showed demand has not wavered, but the share price, which hit a 16-month low on Wednesday, shows investors want answers on governance before they give the new leadership the benefit of the doubt. 

CEO at NVDA Colette Kress had a tought gig right now.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan’s AI stocks lose their premium as three threats emerge after Nvidia’s CEO exit
item.description:
Japan’s AI-linked chip stocks carry heavy weights in the Nikkei 225, so further selling in names like Advantest can drag the headline index more than the broader TOPIX. That explains much of the gap between the two benchmarks this month. A move from premium to discount valuations would be a lasting headwind rather than a one-day shock, and it favours rotation into cheaper domestic sectors such as banks, which also benefit from higher BOJ rates. The yen’s weakness offers exporters some cushion. Chip names, though, are trading on AI sentiment and Nvidia’s governance story more than on currency moves.

-

Japan’s AI chip stocks were priced as can’t-miss growth plays. With profits in question, regulation looming and Nvidia in turmoil, investors are starting to ask for a discount, and the most expensive names look most at risk.

Summary:

  • Japanese stocks that traded at a premium for their AI exposure are now seen by some investors as too risky
  • Kioxia and Advantest have each fallen more than 9% since Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, against an almost 3% drop in the TOPIX
  • Analysts point to a triple hit: weaker profitability, expected tighter regulation after the US midterms, and the Nvidia turmoil
  • Investors may shift from paying a premium for AI exposure to demanding a discount
  • Large AI names still at premium valuations could see more selling, while stocks that have already corrected may be near a bottom

Japanese stocks that had commanded a premium for their exposure to artificial intelligence are now being viewed as too risky by some investors, with Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia adding to doubts about the sector’s outlook, according to market reports on Thursday. Since Huang’s resignation, shares of memory maker Kioxia Holdings and chip testing equipment maker Advantest have each fallen by more than 9%, more than three times the almost 3% decline in the broader TOPIX index over the same period.

Analysts describe AI-linked stocks as facing a triple hit. The first is a worsening profit picture, as questions grow over whether heavy AI spending can deliver adequate returns. The second is the prospect of tighter regulation following the US midterm elections, which revealed a political backlash against the technology. The third is the market turbulence unleashed by the leadership crisis at Nvidia, the industry’s bellwether.

The key shift, analysts say, is in how investors price the theme. For much of the AI boom, Japanese suppliers to the chip industry traded at a premium because of their place in the global supply chain. That willingness to pay up may now be turning into a demand for a discount, as investors weigh the risks rather than the growth story alone.

Not all stocks are seen as equally exposed. Fund managers noted that some of the largest AI-related names still trade at premium valuations, leaving them vulnerable to further selling. By contrast, stocks that have already fallen sharply may be closer to finding a floor, offering potential opportunities for selective buyers.

The reassessment comes at a sensitive time for Japanese equities. The Nikkei 225 has fallen around 7% this month, in large part on concern over whether global AI investment can keep growing at its recent pace, and the Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise interest rates again in December. Strong quarterly results from Nvidia this week failed to stop its shares sliding to a 16-month low, a sign that investors are focusing on governance and valuation risks rather than near-term demand. For Japan’s chip suppliers, that suggests the bar for a sustained recovery has risen. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Lava CEO says bitcoin sellers are spent, but whale exchange flows point the other way
item.description:
Whale exchange deposits are the number to watch. A sustained slowdown would support the argument that sellers are exhausted, while continued net inflows leave any rally exposed to supply from large holders. Listed miners such as MARA and Riot remain a source of spot supply as long as they keep selling their bitcoin, which also clouds the outlook for miner equities. US spot bitcoin ETFs lost roughly $2.1 billion between late October and mid-November, so the long-term buying Maredia describes has yet to show up in fund flows. For wider risk sentiment, the AI rotation idea needs bitcoin to rise on days when AI stocks fall, not simply lag them.

---

Earlier:

  • BlackRock says bitcoin’s fading link to stocks strengthens the case for allocation

--- A bitcoin CEO says the sellers are done, but the largest wallets are still moving coins onto exchanges, so the recovery case rests on a turn in flows that the data has not yet shown.

Summary:

  • Lava CEO Shehzan Maredia argues that miner and whale selling may be largely complete, pointing to the market’s contained reaction to a recent major exchange hack
  • He says long-term holders keep buying despite falling prices, and that stablecoin payments are bringing new users abroad to bitcoin as a savings asset
  • He expects profits from AI investments to rotate into bitcoin, and sees the Democratic election sweep possibly adding regulatory pressure on AI
  • He plays down the Clarity Act’s importance for bitcoin and does not expect another tenfold rally within a year
  • On-chain data shows entities holding 1,000 BTC or more sending about $55 million more to exchanges daily than they withdraw
  • Long-dormant whales booked around $295 million in realised profits on 10 November, their largest profit-taking event of 2026

Lava founder and chief executive Shehzan Maredia believes bitcoin may be nearing a turning point as selling from miners and large holders fades, but on-chain data, which tracks coin movements recorded on the blockchain, suggests the biggest wallets are still adding to supply on exchanges.

Speaking in an interview with Anthony Pompliano, reported by Benzinga, Maredia pointed to three developments he sees as supportive for bitcoin’s longer-term outlook. He argued that miners and whales, the term for holders of very large amounts of bitcoin, may have already done much of their selling, citing the market’s relatively contained response to a recent major exchange hack as evidence. He also said long-term holders have kept buying despite falling prices, and that stablecoin payments are introducing new users abroad to bitcoin as a savings asset. Stablecoins are tokens pegged to a currency such as the US dollar, often used for cross-border transfers.

Maredia expects investors to rotate profits from AI holdings into bitcoin, particularly with equity valuations stretched. In his view, the Democratic election sweep could bring tighter regulatory pressure on AI, which could speed up that shift in capital. He played down the importance of the Clarity Act, US legislation aimed at setting out how crypto markets are regulated, arguing that adoption, network security and savings demand matter more for bitcoin than further market-structure rules.

The flow data is harder to square with the idea that sellers are spent. Entities holding 1,000 BTC or more are sending roughly $55 million more bitcoin to exchanges each day than they withdraw. That matters because coins are usually moved onto an exchange to be sold, while withdrawals into private storage tend to signal an intention to hold. The pattern reverses earlier periods when withdrawals dominated. Separate data showed whales that had held coins for years locking in around $295 million in profits on 10 November, their largest profit-taking event of 2026, with bitcoin near $73,700 at the time.

Supply from listed companies has also been heavy. Fourteen public companies have sold a combined total of about 108,000 BTC this year, worth around $8.1 billion, with miners prominent among the sellers.

Maredia does not expect another tenfold rally within a year. He sees bitcoin maturing into an asset with steadier returns and lower volatility, with the halving, the roughly four-yearly cut in the new bitcoin awarded to miners, still relevant but investor demand and market structure playing a growing role.

The next thing to watch is whether whale exchange deposits begin to slow. A sustained drop would lend weight to Maredia’s case that selling is exhausted, while continued net deposits would suggest large holders are still using rallies to sell. Readers can also track whether spot ETF flows turn positive and whether bitcoin holds up on days when AI stocks fall, which would be the first real evidence of the rotation he describes.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More from Ueda: real rates still low, and BOJ finances can withstand further hikes
item.description:
These follow-up comments matter more for the path beyond December than for the December decision, which already looked well set. By saying real rates are still low and conditions loose, Ueda leaves room for the 1.75% end-March level many economists expect, and possibly more. That supports higher short-dated JGB yields and gives the yen modest support. The reassurance on BOJ finances and ETF sales removes a technical worry that some had seen as a brake on tightening. Japanese equities may watch the ETF comment closely, since the pace of BOJ selling affects a large holder of the market.

---

Earlier:

  • BOJ’s Ueda expects to keep raising rates, warning inflation could overshoot 2% target

---

Ueda used his follow-up remarks to close off the obvious arguments for waiting. Weak spending was expected, firms can handle higher costs, and the BOJ’s own finances aren’t a constraint, all of which leaves the path clear for more hikes.

Summary:

  • Ueda said real interest rates remain low at the short end despite past hikes, and that financial conditions are still loose
  • He said higher funding costs for firms must be weighed against strong earnings and rising wages
  • He said the drop in July to September consumption was within BOJ expectations, and that consumption is resilient overall as wages rise
  • The BOJ will scrutinise how hikes affect corporate and household activity
  • Ueda said BOJ simulations suggest its policy, including accelerated ETF sales, need not severely damage its finances

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda added detail to his case for further rate hikes on Thursday, arguing that real interest rates remain low despite past increases and that strong corporate earnings and rising wages should help the economy absorb higher borrowing costs. His latest comments, which crossed the wires between 01:17 and 01:35 GMT, followed earlier remarks in which he said the BOJ expects to keep raising rates and warned that underlying inflation could overshoot its 2% target.

Ueda acknowledged that rate hikes push up funding costs for companies, but said any assessment of their impact must also weigh healthy profits and steadily rising pay. Even after the BOJ’s earlier moves, he said, real interest rates remain low at the shorter end of the curve, the part that matters most for economic activity, and overall financial conditions are still loose and supportive. The bank will closely examine how higher rates affect corporate and household behaviour, he added.

He also sought to defuse concern over the weak spot in the latest growth figures. The drop in consumption in the July to September quarter, as shown in the GDP data, was within the BOJ’s expectations, Ueda said, describing consumption as resilient overall as wages climb steadily in a tight labour market. That matters because the unexpected contraction in third-quarter GDP had raised questions about whether the BOJ would pause.

On the central bank’s own balance sheet, Ueda said internal simulations suggest the BOJ can avoid a situation in which its policy, including accelerated sales of its exchange-traded fund holdings, inflicts severe damage on its finances. The issue has drawn attention because higher rates increase the interest the BOJ pays on banks’ reserves while much of its bond portfolio still carries low yields, squeezing its income. Ueda’s reassurance signals that balance sheet worries are not a constraint on further tightening.

Taken together, the comments strip away several possible reasons for the BOJ to hold back in December: weak consumption, corporate funding costs and the bank’s own finances. With real rates still low and financial conditions loose by Ueda’s own assessment, the bar to keep hiking appears low. Markets will look to Japan’s national CPI data at 23:30 GMT on Thursday for further confirmation ahead of the December 17 to 18 meeting. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ’s Ueda expects to keep raising rates, warning inflation could overshoot 2% target
item.description:
Ueda’s remarks firm up the case for a December hike, which should give some support to the yen, although the effect may be limited while the Fed is also raising rates. The emphasis on overshoot risk could matter more for the path beyond December, supporting bets on a move to 1.75% by March and keeping upward pressure on short-dated JGB yields. Japanese bank stocks tend to benefit from a steeper rate path, while exporters lose some of the support from a weak yen. Overnight inflation data will be the next catalyst. A firm print would strengthen expectations for both the December move and the one after it.

---

Earlier:

  • BOJ tipped to hike to 1.50% in December, its first three-hike year in 37 years

---

Ueda’s worry is no longer inflation falling short of 2%. It’s inflation overshooting, and with policy still accommodative, that points to more hikes, starting in December.

Summary:

  • BOJ Governor Ueda said the bank expects to keep raising rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative
  • He warned of a risk that underlying inflation could overshoot the 2% target
  • Ueda said underlying inflation is roughly consistent with the target and that anchoring it around 2% is important
  • He described the economy as recovering moderately with some weakness, and consumption as resilient
  • A Reuters poll shows 86% of economists expect a hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting
  • National CPI data for October are due at 23:30 GMT on Thursday

Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Thursday that the central bank expects to keep raising interest rates because monetary conditions remain accommodative, adding that there is a risk underlying inflation could overshoot the BOJ’s 2% target. His remarks, which crossed the wires from 01:03 GMT, reinforce expectations of a December hike and come a day after he said the bank should continue lifting borrowing costs.

Ueda described the economy as recovering moderately, albeit with some weakness, and said consumption has been resilient. He judged underlying inflation to be roughly consistent with the price target, but stressed that the bigger danger now lies on the upside. Anchoring underlying inflation around 2%, he said, is important to stop the risk of an overshoot from materialising.

That framing matters. For years the BOJ’s challenge was getting inflation up to target. Ueda is now signalling that the task has flipped to keeping it from running too far above it, and that with real interest rates still negative, policy is far from restrictive. In that light, further hikes look less like tightening for its own sake and more like the gradual removal of stimulus that the economy no longer needs.

The comments sit comfortably with market expectations. In a Reuters poll published on Wednesday, 86% of economists forecast a 25 basis point hike to 1.50% at the December 17 to 18 meeting, which would be the BOJ’s third increase this year, and nearly 60% expect another move to 1.75% by the end of March. Ueda’s description of consumption as resilient also offers some cover for pressing ahead despite the economy’s unexpected contraction in the July to September quarter.

The weak yen remains a key part of the backdrop. The currency is trading near 160 per dollar despite heavy intervention by Japanese authorities this year, and a widening rate gap with a Federal Reserve that is itself still hiking keeps pressure on the BOJ to act. A weak yen raises import costs and adds to the very inflation overshoot risk Ueda highlighted.

The next test comes quickly. Japan’s national consumer price data for October are due at 23:30 GMT on Thursday, and a firm reading would further strengthen the case for a December move. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock says bitcoin’s fading link to stocks strengthens the case for allocation
item.description:
The diversification pitch arrives at a fragile point for bitcoin flows. US spot ETFs lost roughly $2.1 billion between late October and mid-November, so a turn back to steady inflows would be the clearest sign that allocators are buying BlackRock’s argument. Strategy faces an extra technical overhang from its scheduled removal from MSCI indexes on 30 November, which could weigh on MSTR and on spot demand around the rebalance. Ether has tracked equities at least as closely as bitcoin this year, which limits how far the decoupling story reaches across the wider crypto complex. For risk sentiment, the signal to watch is how bitcoin behaves on the next sharp equity down day, not whether it keeps lagging a rally.

--- BlackRock is selling bitcoin as the asset that zigs when stocks zag, but November’s decoupling has mostly meant bitcoin missing the rebound, which is not quite the hedge allocators are being promised.

Summary:

  • BlackRock’s global head of digital assets, Robbie Mitchnick, says bitcoin’s correlation with equities has fallen substantially after a period of sharp interest rate moves
  • He argues that a move back toward zero correlation would strengthen the case for portfolio allocation
  • He says bitcoin has moved almost inversely to the AI trade, up about 30% since 30 June while AI names are down around 20%
  • Government debt and deficit worries, made worse by higher rates, are pushing debasement-wary investors toward bitcoin as a more volatile alternative to gold
  • The minimum for in-kind conversions into ETF shares has dropped to about $1 million from $30 million, and a new bitcoin premium income product has passed $100 million
  • Earlier this month, bitcoin’s 30-day correlation with the S&P 500 hit around 0.8, the highest since 2020

BlackRock’s top digital assets executive has renewed the case for holding bitcoin in diversified portfolios, arguing that its link to the stock market has weakened substantially and that a return toward zero correlation would make the allocation argument stronger for many investors.

Robbie Mitchnick, global head of digital assets at the world’s largest asset manager, made the comments in an interview with Anthony Pompliano on 18 November, as reported by TokenPost. He said bitcoin’s correlation with equities had dropped substantially after a period of sharp interest rate changes, and that the cryptocurrency had moved almost inversely to the AI trade, a pattern he described as useful for portfolio construction. By his measure, bitcoin has gained about 30% since 30 June while the AI trade has fallen roughly 20%, though he acknowledged that tracking the AI trade is an imprecise exercise.

Mitchnick also pointed to fiscal strain as a source of demand. Higher interest rates are adding to governments’ debt burdens, he said, and that is drawing investors worried about currency debasement and inflation toward bitcoin. Gold has long been the default hedge for those concerns, but in his view more investors are now weighing bitcoin as a more volatile alternative with greater potential upside and downside.

BlackRock is widening the ways investors can hold the asset. Mitchnick said the minimum for in-kind conversions of bitcoin into ETF shares has dropped to about $1 million from $30 million, and that a new bitcoin premium income product passed $100 million in its first couple of months.

The decorrelation argument is not new for the firm. Mitchnick has maintained since at least 2024 that bitcoin’s long-run correlation with stocks sits close to zero, and BlackRock’s guidance of a 1% to 2% allocation in multi-asset portfolios rests on the same idea. As issuer of the iShares Bitcoin Trust, the firm also has a direct commercial interest in the case.

The timing is what makes the latest remarks notable. Analytics data showed bitcoin’s 30-day correlation with the S&P 500 reaching around 0.8 earlier this month, the highest since 2020, as the cryptocurrency fell alongside equities in the early November selloff. Longer-run figures put the correlation at 0.29 since 2018, rising to roughly 0.50 this year.

The link has since loosened, but mostly on the downside, with bitcoin sitting out the latest relief rally in US stocks. For allocators weighing BlackRock’s pitch, the real test is whether low correlation holds when equities fall, which is when a diversifier earns its place in a portfolio.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Musk wants Tesla’s best-selling car to lose its steering wheel. The ambition is real and the Cybercab shows the technology is on the road, but until there’s a date, it’s direction, not delivery.

Summary:

  • Musk says Tesla will produce a fully self-driving Model Y with no steering wheel or pedals
  • No timeline, pricing or production details were given
  • The two-seat Cybercab, which has no manual controls, began paid rides in Austin in September
  • Musk pushed for a wheel-free Model Y years ago before executives talked him out of it
  • His past autonomy targets, including one million robotaxis by 2020, were missed

Elon Musk says Tesla will produce a fully self-driving version of the Model Y with no steering wheel or pedals, extending the controls-free design of its Cybercab robotaxi to the company’s best-selling vehicle. No timeline, pricing or production details were given.

The idea itself is not new. Tesla’s two-seat Cybercab, built without a steering wheel or pedals, began carrying paying passengers in Austin in September and made up about half of the company’s Texas robotaxi fleet by the end of October. Musk has also wanted a controls-free Model Y for years: a 2021 book on the company reported that he pushed for the original Model Y to launch without a steering wheel before executives steered him away from it.

What would be new is scale. A driverless Model Y would offer a larger, family-sized vehicle for Tesla’s ride-hailing ambitions and potentially for private buyers, rather than a niche two-seater.

Investors have reason for caution. Musk’s autonomy targets have a long history of slipping, most famously his 2019 prediction of one million robotaxis on the road by 2020. Selling cars with no manual controls widely would also require regulatory approval well beyond what a limited robotaxi service needs. Until Tesla attaches a date, a production plan or regulatory progress to the statement, it is best read as a statement of direction rather than a product launch.

item.title: Australian unemployment jumps to 4.9% as jobs fall 43,500, taking RBA hikes off the table
item.description:
The Australian dollar is the clearest loser. It has broken below 0.6700 and now faces a widening policy gap, with the RBA likely done while four Fed officials argued for more hikes just yesterday. If that divergence holds, AUD/USD is exposed to further downside. Front-end Australian government bond yields should fall as hike pricing for February is removed, and rate-sensitive ASX sectors such as banks, property and consumer discretionary could find some support from a lower rate outlook. The catch is inflation above 4%, kept elevated by energy costs. That leaves the RBA unable to cut, a stagflation-tinged mix that gives the Aussie little support from either side.

---

The 'just the data' post on this is here:

  • Australian unemployment rate jumps to 4.9% in October, against 4.7% expected

---

Two straight months of job losses have pushed Australia’s unemployment rate to 4.9%, effectively ending the RBA’s tightening cycle at 4.85%. The question now is how long rates stay there, not how much higher they go.

Summary:

  • Australia’s unemployment rate rose to 4.9% in October, against 4.7% expected and 4.7% prior, the highest since late 2021
  • Employment fell 43,500, against a forecast 25,000 gain, after a 39,300 drop in September
  • Part-time jobs fell 40,600 and full-time jobs slipped 2,900
  • Participation fell to 66.6% from 66.8%, so unemployment rose even as fewer people looked for work
  • Unemployment has already reached the RBA’s end-2026 forecast, backing the three board members who opposed November’s hike
  • The Australian dollar fell below 0.6700

Australia’s unemployment rate jumped to 4.9% in October from 4.7%, well above the 4.7% economists had expected, as employment fell for a second straight month, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday. Employment dropped by 43,500, against forecasts for a gain of 25,000, after a 39,300 fall in September. The jobless rate is now the highest since late 2021.

The detail offered little comfort. Economists had expected September’s slump in part-time work to reverse, but part-time employment fell by a further 40,600, while full-time jobs slipped by 2,900 after rising in September. Taken together, the economy has shed more than 80,000 jobs in two months. Unemployment rose even though the participation rate fell to 66.6% from 66.8%. That combination is unusually weak: fewer people were looking for work, yet the share of those who could not find it still climbed.

The result lands squarely in the middle of the Reserve Bank of Australia’s internal debate. Minutes released on Tuesday showed three of nine board members voted against November’s hike to 4.85%, warning the economy might be close to a materially sharper downturn and pointing to a larger-than-expected rise in unemployment. Thursday’s data give that minority fresh ammunition. The RBA’s own forecasts had unemployment reaching 4.9% only by the end of this year, so the labour market has deteriorated faster than the central bank assumed.

The problem for the RBA is that inflation has not gone away. Headline inflation is running above 4%, and data on Wednesday showed annual wage growth of 3.5% in the September quarter, with the quarterly rise the largest since late 2023. The majority on the board judged rates were not yet clearly high enough to contain upside inflation risks, and that concern will not disappear simply because of a weak run of jobs data.

Even so, two consecutive monthly declines in employment should take further rate hikes off the table. A December move was already largely priced out before the release, and it is now hard to see the board tightening into a labour market that is shedding jobs this quickly. February, which some economists had flagged as the next realistic window for a hike, looks to have closed as well. The question for the RBA has shifted from how much further rates need to rise to how long they stay at 4.85%, and with unemployment rising faster than forecast, the conversation could turn to when cuts come onto the agenda if the weakness persists.

The Australian dollar fell on the data, slipping below 0.6700 and below the 10-month low it touched earlier in the week.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
