item.title: Four Fed officials push for more hikes as Waller floats 50bp to break 3% inflation mindset
item.description:
The combined message supports the dollar and keeps front-end Treasury yields firm, though markets aren’t chasing Waller’s call for a bigger move. That leaves room for a repricing if December data run hot. If Waller’s communication-first approach wins out, the risk is a more hawkish statement and press conference even with a 25bp hike, which could push expectations for the rate path higher. Gold faces a headwind from rising hike expectations, as it has throughout this cycle. Rate-sensitive AI and growth stocks remain exposed after a bruising week. Elevated oil prices are part of the inflation problem the hawks describe, so energy remains the swing factor for how far they push.

--- Wednesday’s Fed speakers agreed that inflation needs more work. The only real disagreement is pace: Waller wants a bigger hike or much tougher guidance, while the rest appear content with steady quarter-point steps.

Summary:

  • Governor Waller favours a 50bp hike in December or much tougher forward guidance to break the public’s acceptance of 3% inflation
  • Waller noted that about 70% of core services components are running above 3% and said the Fed may need to go beyond reversing last year’s cuts
  • Kashkari said markets expect more hikes than officials do and stressed keeping inflation expectations anchored
  • Daly said inflation has been too high for too long, with spending resilient even among lower-income households
  • Barr supports further hikes if the economy evolves as expected but gave no timetable
  • Markets price about 61bp of hikes over three meetings, with only around a 5% chance of a 50bp move in December

Four Federal Reserve policymakers lined up on Wednesday to argue that the fight against inflation is not finished, with Governor Christopher Waller going furthest by making the case for a 50 basis point hike in December. Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari, San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly and Governor Michael Barr all leaned the same way, pointing to inflation that has stayed too high for too long against a backdrop of resilient spending and a stable jobs market. Together, their remarks reinforce expectations that the Fed will raise rates again next month, with the debate now centred on how hard to push rather than whether to move.

Waller: break the 3% psychology

Waller set out the most aggressive view. He is worried that price pressures have spread well beyond energy, noting that roughly 70% of the components in the core services basket are running above 3%. He sees businesses growing comfortable passing higher costs on to customers, partly because they believe consumers can absorb them, and fears the public is starting to accept inflation around 3% as normal after years above the Fed’s 2% target.

To break that psychology, Waller believes the Fed needs to act more forcefully, either by raising rates by 50 basis points in December or by signalling a markedly tougher stance through statements, press conferences and forward guidance. He suggested the Fed may need to go beyond simply reversing the rate cuts it made last year, and questioned how useful the December economic projections will be, preferring sharper forward-looking communication. Waller is, for now, alone among governors in pushing for a bigger move, but his views have often been an early signal of where policy goes next.

Kashkari: markets see more hikes than officials do

Kashkari’s most striking comment was that markets believe the Fed will need to raise rates further than officials currently expect, and he made no effort to talk that pricing down. He traced elevated inflation to a series of supply shocks and said keeping inflation expectations anchored is essential. He described the strength of demand as somewhat surprising and the job market as resilient, and said higher rates can clearly weigh on investment.

Daly: too high for too long

Daly described the labour market as stable but lacking dynamism, with employment broad-based and helped by a revival in manufacturing. She said consumer spending remains resilient, even among lower-income households, and that inflation has been too high for too long, while acknowledging uncertainty over how it will evolve. Last week she said further hikes were likely needed, citing inflation spreading into services, though she also noted early signs of consumer fatigue and plans to watch holiday spending closely.

Barr: more hikes if the outlook holds

Barr said he would support further rate increases if the economy evolves as he expects, calling inflation too high and a strain on many households. He described the economy as strong with low unemployment and said returning inflation to 2% in a timely way is critical, though he declined to commit to a timetable.

What markets are pricing

Markets were pricing around 61 basis points of hikes over the next three meetings, consistent with a quarter point move in December and more to follow. A 50 basis point step in December, however, was given only about a 5% chance, suggesting traders see Waller’s call as a warning shot rather than the base case. Minutes of the Fed’s last meeting, released on Wednesday, were reported to show officials expect further hikes and are concerned that AI investment could add to inflation, which fits the tone set by all four speakers. 

The collective noun for hawks seems to be a "Fed" right now. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6684 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan machinery orders up 13.4% y/y: what this early capex signal tells you
item.description:
Machinery orders rarely move the yen or Japanese stocks on release, and this print, broadly in line with forecasts, is unlikely to be an exception. For rates traders, firm investment demand slightly strengthens the case that Japan’s economy can absorb further BOJ tightening, despite the third-quarter contraction. Equipment makers and factory automation stocks are the most direct beneficiaries if the trend holds. Bigger tests for the yen come from inflation data and the BOJ meeting itself.

---

Earlier:

  • BOJ tipped to hike to 1.50% in December, its first three-hike year in 37 years

---

Japan’s machinery orders are one of the economy’s earliest signals of business investment. September’s double-digit annual gain suggests firms are still spending on equipment while consumers and GDP falter.

Summary:

  • Japan’s core machinery orders rose 13.4% y/y in September, against 13.7% expected and 18.6% in August
  • Orders fell 0.3% m/m, a smaller drop than the 0.5% forecast, after a 5.2% gain in August
  • The data track orders for capital equipment and lead actual business investment by several months
  • “Core” orders exclude ships and electric power companies, whose large one-off contracts distort the total
  • Monthly readings are volatile, so economists focus on annual rates or three-month averages
  • Firm capex demand supports the view that Japan can absorb the December BOJ rate hike that’s widely expected

Japan’s core machinery orders rose 13.4% in September from a year earlier, a touch below the 13.7% gain economists had expected and down from August’s 18.6% jump, but still a strong double-digit annual increase. On the month, orders slipped 0.3%, a smaller fall than the 0.5% decline forecast, after rising 5.2% in August. The Cabinet Office data were released at 23:50 GMT on Wednesday (6:50 pm US Eastern).

The numbers point to business investment demand that remains firm rather than fading, even as the wider economy stumbles. To see why that matters, it helps to understand what this indicator measures and how to read it.

What machinery orders measure

Machinery orders track the value of orders that Japanese machinery makers receive for equipment such as industrial machines, computers, communication gear and other capital goods. Because companies place orders before the equipment is built, delivered and installed, the data act as an early signal of future capital expenditure, typically leading actual business investment by several months.

The headline figure that markets watch is “core” orders, which strip out orders for ships and orders from electric power companies. Those categories involve large, infrequent contracts that can swing the total sharply from one month to the next without saying much about the broader trend. Removing them gives a cleaner read on private-sector demand for equipment.

Why the monthly figure is so noisy

Even the core series is notoriously volatile. A handful of big orders can push a single month up or down by several percentage points, which is why August’s 5.2% monthly surge was followed by a small dip in September. Economists generally focus on the year-on-year rate or on a three-month average rather than any single monthly print. On that basis, September’s result keeps the trend clearly positive: annual growth has stayed in double digits for two months running.

Why it matters

Capital spending is one of the main engines of Japan’s economy, and it is a key test of whether firms are confident enough to invest despite higher borrowing costs. That makes the data relevant to the Bank of Japan, which is widely expected to raise interest rates again in December even though the economy unexpectedly contracted in the July to September quarter. Firm orders suggest companies are still putting money into automation, digital upgrades and capacity, partly to cope with labour shortages, which supports the BOJ’s view that the economy can absorb further tightening.

That said, the indicator rarely moves markets on its own. It is a supporting piece of evidence rather than a headline event, and its real value is in confirming or questioning the trend that other data, such as the quarterly Tankan business survey and GDP figures, are showing.

What to watch next

The Cabinet Office also publishes quarterly outlooks for orders, which give a forward look at how manufacturers expect demand to develop. Alongside Japan’s nationwide inflation data, due at 23:30 GMT on Thursday, and the BOJ’s December 17 to 18 meeting, those will help show whether resilient investment can offset weaker consumption and keep the case for higher rates intact. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic confirms $83 IPO price on 980 million shares in an $81 billion deal
item.description:
The size of the deal is the main market story. Absorbing roughly $81 billion of new stock, and potentially more if the over-allotment option is used, draws liquidity from elsewhere. That could weigh on other AI and mega-cap tech names in the short term as funds rebalance to make room. A strong debut would likely help neocloud and AI infrastructure stocks, which sold off this week on funding worries, while a weak one would reinforce them. The over-allotment option also gives underwriters a tool to support the price in the early days of trading, which may soften any initial volatility.

---

Anthropic’s official numbers confirm a deal of extraordinary size, with roughly $79 billion going straight to the company. Whether public markets can digest it will be clear once ANT opens on Thursday.

Summary:

  • Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share (earlier tip on this), above the $70 to $78 range, selling 980 million Class A shares
  • About 956 million shares are new, raising roughly $79 billion for Anthropic, and selling stockholders are offering about 24 million shares
  • Underwriters have a 30-day option to buy up to 147 million more shares, which would take the deal to about $93.5 billion
  • Trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT is due to begin Thursday, November 19, with no scheduled time for the first trade
  • The offering is expected to close on November 20, and the announcement gave no valuation or use of proceeds

Anthropic has confirmed the pricing of its initial public offering at $83 per share, selling 980 million Class A shares in a deal worth around $81 billion before any additional shares are sold, the company said in an announcement on Wednesday. Trading is due to begin on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19. As with any IPO, there is no scheduled time for the first trade: the stock opens once enough buy and sell orders have been matched to set an opening price, which can happen anywhere from minutes to hours after the regular session begins.

Most of the shares on offer are new. Anthropic is selling about 956 million shares itself, which at the offer price would raise roughly $79 billion for the company, while existing shareholders are selling about 24 million shares, worth around $2 billion. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the shares sold by those stockholders. The underwriters also have a 30-day option to buy up to 147 million additional shares, equal to 15% of the base deal. If that option is exercised in full, the total offering would rise to around $93.5 billion.

The $83 price sits above the $70 to $78 range Anthropic set last week, a sign that institutional demand outstripped the shares on offer. The Securities and Exchange Commission declared the registration statement effective on Wednesday, and the offering is expected to close on Friday, November 20, subject to customary conditions. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are named in the announcement as sources for copies of the final prospectus.

The company’s announcement did not set out a valuation or say how it plans to use the money. It did restate that Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, with a stated mission of developing and maintaining advanced AI responsibly for the long-term benefit of humanity. That structure gives the board a legal duty to weigh its mission alongside shareholder returns, a point new investors will need to factor in when judging how the company balances growth, safety and profit.

The scale of the raise is striking even by the standards of the AI boom, and it arrives at a fragile moment. AI stocks have been hit in recent days by worries over rising interest rates, new US curbs on chip sales and the leadership crisis at Nvidia, whose shares fell to a 16-month low on Wednesday. How ANT trades on its first day will be read well beyond Anthropic: a firm debut would suggest public markets are still willing to fund the AI build-out at scale, while a weak one would add to the doubts that have been building across the sector. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Moody’s keeps US rating at Aa1 as the economy beats forecasts, seeing 2.3% growth this year
item.description:
A stable Aa1 outlook removes one source of headline risk for Treasuries, but the growth upgrade cuts the other way for bonds. Stronger-than-expected activity strengthens the hawkish case being made by Fed officials this week and supports pricing for a December hike, which should keep front-end yields and the dollar firm. That’s a headwind for gold, which has tended to fall as Fed hike expectations build. Moody’s flagged energy prices as a drag on growth, a reminder that oil is the swing factor: further strength in crude would hurt growth and keep inflation pressure alive at the same time.

--

Moody’s says the US economy has outperformed, and it’s leaving the rating alone. But it expects the things that drove this year’s strength, cheap money aside, to fade as higher rates, costly energy and a maturing AI boom slow growth to about 2%.

Summary:

  • Moody’s kept the US sovereign rating at Aa1 with a stable outlook after its regular review
  • The agency said the economy has outperformed its expectations, with Q3 real GDP growth of 3.4% annualised
  • Growth is forecast at 2.3% this year, then around 2% in both 2027 and 2028
  • AI infrastructure spending is supporting near-term growth and may lift productivity, though the scale of the gains is uncertain
  • Higher interest rates, elevated energy prices and a normalising AI investment cycle are seen as drags on growth
  • Moody’s cited innovation, a dynamic private sector, deep capital markets, the dollar’s reserve status and an independent Fed as key strengths

Moody’s Ratings said the US economy has performed better than it initially expected in 2026, and it kept the country’s Aa1 sovereign rating with a stable outlook in its regular review of US creditworthiness. The agency pointed to real GDP growth of 3.4% at an annualised pace in the third quarter and now expects growth of 2.3% for the full year, before a slowdown to around 2% in both 2027 and 2028.

Artificial intelligence features on both sides of that outlook. Moody’s said heavy spending on AI infrastructure is propping up growth in the near term and could eventually deliver lasting productivity gains, although it stressed that the size of those gains is still uncertain. At the same time, it expects the AI investment cycle to normalise, which would remove some of the support that has driven this year’s outperformance.

The agency listed two other headwinds alongside that: higher interest rates and energy prices that remain elevated. Both are live issues. Several Federal Reserve officials have argued this week for further tightening, and oil markets remain on edge over shipping risks in the Middle East. Against those pressures, Moody’s said the economy’s capacity for innovation, a dynamic private sector and deep capital markets should continue to support investment and productivity over time.

The rating rationale leans heavily on institutional strengths. Moody’s cited the country’s very high creditworthiness, its resilience to shocks and the dollar’s role as the world’s reserve currency. It also said it expects the US to maintain its long record of effective monetary policy led by an independent Federal Reserve. That point is more than a formality: Fed independence is one of the pillars the rating rests on, so any perceived erosion of it would sit squarely within what the agency is watching.

For investors, the review offers reassurance without much drama. A stable outlook signals that Moody’s sees no near-term pressure for a change in either direction, and its growth forecasts broadly match the picture of an economy that is running hotter than expected but set to cool as rates bite and the AI spending surge matures. The bigger question for markets is whether that late-year strength keeps the Fed on its hiking path into December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS says the AI sell-off is a reset, not a collapse, and backs eurozone stocks and bonds
item.description:
The UBS view gives some support to dip-buyers, but how much it helps depends on the breadth test it sets. As long as selling stays concentrated in chips, neoclouds and richly valued growth names, the bank’s case holds. A spread into banks and industrials would challenge it. Rates are the main threat. With four Fed officials sounding hawkish on Wednesday alone and Treasury yields already elevated, financing pressure on leveraged AI infrastructure is likely to stay in focus. The tilt toward Europe and short-dated quality bonds suggests investors may rotate within markets rather than exit them. Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut today is an early real-time read on whether risk appetite for AI is holding up.

--- UBS thinks the AI boom is being repriced, not unwound, and its advice is to stay invested but spread the risk across sectors, regions and bonds while watching utilisation and returns rather than chip orders.

Summary:

  • UBS says recent tech volatility reflects a positioning and valuation adjustment and doesn’t change its constructive view on equities over six to 12 months
  • It forecasts AI capital spending of $1.0 trillion in 2026, $1.4 trillion in 2027 and $1.5 trillion in 2028, mostly from well-funded platforms
  • New US chip curbs could affect 5% to 10% of next year’s AI demand, but the revenue hit to US chipmakers should be limited
  • What would change UBS’s view: weaker compute demand, slower AI revenue growth, poor utilisation, tighter financing for the biggest platforms, or selling spreading into cyclical sectors
  • UBS favours tech platforms with real AI revenue and strong balance sheets, plus US health care and industrials, eurozone equities and high-quality short- and medium-dated bonds
  • Since the note, Nvidia has slid to a 16-month low despite beating forecasts, and four Fed officials have struck hawkish notes

UBS is urging investors to stay engaged with the AI theme rather than run for cover, arguing that the recent turbulence in technology stocks looks like a reset in positioning and valuations, not the start of a collapse in AI investment. In a note to clients, the bank said volatility has not shaken its conviction in the structural AI opportunity or its constructive view on diversified equities, and it still sees room for broad market gains over the next six to 12 months.

A rough week for the AI trade

The note was written after a sharp sell-off on Monday, when US curbs on offshore data centres buying American chips and a cautious speech from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh on the risks of an AI investment bust hit chip stocks hard. The pressure has not let up since. Nvidia beat forecasts on Tuesday, with revenue of around $116 billion and guidance for roughly $130 billion this quarter, yet its shares fell about 3% on Wednesday to a 16-month low as investors focused on the leadership vacuum left by Jensen Huang’s resignation and a reported Securities and Exchange Commission investigation. The S&P 500 fell for a fifth straight session.

Rates added to the strain. Four Fed officials, Neel Kashkari, Christopher Waller, Mary Daly and Michael Barr, all struck hawkish notes on Wednesday, with Waller again floating the idea of a 50 basis point hike. That matters for AI because higher borrowing costs weigh most heavily on the more leveraged infrastructure builders.

Why UBS isn’t calling the top

UBS argues that demand for computing capacity remains robust, pointing to accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders. It forecasts total AI capital spending of $1.0 trillion in 2026, $1.4 trillion in 2027 and $1.5 trillion in 2028. Crucially, most of that spending comes from large, well-funded technology platforms, which should limit the damage if weaker, debt-heavy infrastructure providers run into trouble. Delays, repricing and consolidation look more likely to the bank than a broad collapse in spending.

On the new chip restrictions, UBS estimates the rule could affect 5% to 10% of next year’s AI demand, but expects only a limited revenue hit for US chipmakers because supply remains tight and displaced capacity can be sold elsewhere. The bigger risk, it said, is that the rule adds pressure to already elevated 2028 spending and earnings expectations. Smaller cloud and regional data centre operators, along with standalone Chinese AI labs, look most exposed, while the major hyperscalers appear relatively insulated.

What to watch in AI

The bank’s message is that the bar has risen. With cumulative AI investment running into the trillions, investors are now judging the build-out on revenue, free cash flow, utilisation and sustainable returns, not just chip demand. Signs that new computing capacity is being absorbed by rising usage would support confidence. Weaker utilisation, slowing customer commitments or difficulty turning investment into revenue would revive fears of overcapacity.

UBS also set out what would change its view: weakening compute demand, slowing AI revenue growth, poor capacity use, or tighter financial conditions forcing the biggest platforms to cut back. Breadth is the other tell. Selling that stays concentrated in chips, data centre names and richly valued growth stocks fits a valuation adjustment. Selling that spreads into financials, industrials and other cyclical sectors, alongside weaker economic, credit or earnings data, would point to something broader. In the bank’s view, the evidence does not yet support that conclusion.

Where UBS sees opportunity

Rather than turning defensive, UBS advises selectivity. It favours established technology platforms with real AI revenue, existing computing capacity, strong balance sheets and the ability to fund investment internally, and suggests investors with outsized positions in single tech names use rallies to reduce concentration. Within the US, its preferred sectors are health care and industrials.

Beyond the US, the bank remains positive on eurozone equities, where valuations are lower and earnings are supported by a manufacturing recovery and structural investment. It also suggests investors who are significantly underweight bonds rebuild exposure to short- and medium-dated high-quality debt, where elevated yields offer income and diversification. Broad commodities and selected alternatives round out a multi-asset core designed to keep investors in the market while softening the blow from further tech volatility. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Moody’s cuts Nvidia outlook to stable, saying Huang’s exit clouds strategy and policy
item.description:
On its own, an outlook change rarely moves equity prices, and Nvidia’s balance sheet remains among the strongest in corporate credit. The bigger signal is for bond and CDS investors: protection costs had already climbed as the leadership crisis unfolded, and Moody’s move confirms that governance risk is now being priced into Nvidia’s credit. For the wider AI trade, it is another headwind in a week already focused on Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut and Fed rate risk. Asian suppliers such as TSMC and the memory makers could be sensitive to any sign that Nvidia’s partners are rethinking their ties to the company.

---

Moody’s isn’t questioning Nvidia’s ability to pay its debts, but it is now waiting to see who leads the company and how the board’s investigation ends before it considers an upgrade.

Summary:

  • Moody’s lowered Nvidia’s outlook to stable from positive and called the CEO resignation credit negative
  • The agency cited uncertainty over business strategy and financial policies, and possible knock-on effects for Nvidia’s AI partnerships
  • Moody’s also pointed to governance and operational vulnerabilities, including those linked to export controls
  • Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and director on November 11, effective immediately, after 33 years at the company
  • CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and Harvey Jones has been named the board’s first-ever chair
  • The board opened an independent investigation after reports about Huang’s personal conduct, but said it had no reason to believe secrets or national security had been compromised

Moody’s has lowered its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive, saying the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang is credit negative because it has created uncertainty over the chipmaker’s business strategy and financial policies. The change takes a near-term upgrade off the table rather than signalling any weakness in Nvidia’s balance sheet, but it is a pointed signal that the rating agency sees governance, not demand, as the main question hanging over the AI industry’s dominant chip supplier.

Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member on November 11, effective immediately, ending a 33-year run at the company he co-founded. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while keeping her finance role, and the board has appointed Harvey Jones as its first-ever chair while it searches for a permanent successor. The departure followed reports about Huang’s personal conduct, including an alleged link to a person said to have ties to Chinese intelligence, which led the board to open an independent investigation. The board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security had been compromised.

Moody’s concern goes beyond the change at the top. The agency said the leadership shake-up could also weigh on Nvidia’s growth strategy, which relies heavily on a vast web of relationships across the AI industry, at a time when the company is working to fix governance and operational weak spots, including those linked to US export controls. That last point matters because export rules have already shaped Nvidia’s access to China, and any perception that its controls or oversight fall short could invite closer scrutiny from Washington.

A positive outlook typically means a rating agency sees a meaningful chance of an upgrade within the next year or two. Moving back to stable suggests Moody’s now wants to see who leads Nvidia, how the board’s review concludes and whether the company’s partnerships hold up before it considers a higher rating.

The timing is awkward for the AI trade. Investors are already uneasy about rising interest rates and the cost of funding data centre expansion, and Nvidia sits at the centre of that spending. The next markers to watch are the outcome of the board’s investigation, the choice of a permanent chief executive and any sign that customers or partners are rethinking their ties to the company. 

The torch has passed to Colette Kress, Nvidia's new CEO. It's a tough gig right now. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ tipped to hike to 1.50% in December, its first three-hike year in 37 years
item.description:
With a December hike now the clear consensus, the bigger surprise for the yen would be a hold. That would likely send USD/JPY back toward the levels that prompted heavy intervention. A hike on its own may do little to lift the yen while the Fed is also tightening, so traders are likely to focus on whether Ueda signals the faster path to 1.75% that the poll now expects. Front-end JGB yields have room to rise further if that guidance comes through. The Nikkei faces a double headwind from higher domestic rates and the shaky AI trade, which leaves exporters relying more heavily on a weak yen for support.

--- Japan’s economy is shrinking and its stock market is sliding, but with inflation above target and the yen near 160, economists expect the BOJ to keep hiking, first in December and again by March.

Summary:

  • 86% of economists in a Reuters poll, 61 of 71, expect the BOJ to raise rates 25bp to 1.50% at its December 17 to 18 meeting
  • That would be the first time in 37 years that the BOJ has hiked three times in one calendar year
  • Nearly 60% see a further rise to 1.75% by end-March, three months earlier than forecast in October, and views on the peak are split between 1.75% and 2% or higher
  • Governor Ueda said rates should keep rising, after core inflation returned above 2% in September despite a July to September GDP contraction
  • The yen is back near 160 per dollar despite close to $100 billion in intervention, and 83% of economists said the Nikkei’s 7% monthly drop would not derail a hike
  • Next year’s spring wage talks are expected to deliver around 5.00%, close to this year’s 5.01%

The Bank of Japan is expected to raise interest rates at its December 17 to 18 meeting and again by the end of March, according to a Reuters poll published on Wednesday, with policymakers judged to be more worried about inflation and a weak yen than about a stumbling economy. Of 71 economists surveyed between November 11 and 18, 61, or 86%, expect the overnight call rate to rise by 25 basis points to 1.50%, three months after the bank’s last move.

That would mark the BOJ’s third hike of 2026, the first time in 37 years it has tightened three times in a single calendar year. The momentum does not stop there. Nearly 60% of respondents expect another quarter point increase to 1.75% by the end of March, three months sooner than economists forecast in October. Opinion on the end point is split down the middle: among those who answered a separate question, about half see 1.75% as the peak, while an equal share expect rates to reach 2% or higher.

The case for pressing on rests on prices and the currency rather than growth. Japan’s economy unexpectedly shrank in the July to September quarter, its first contraction in a year, yet core consumer inflation rose back above the 2% target in September for the first time in nine months. Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the central bank should keep raising rates. One economist in the poll said the BOJ still sees large upside risks to prices while financial conditions remain loose, and expects policy to stay on a tightening track.

The yen is the sharpest pressure point. It is back near 160 per dollar even after authorities spent close to $100 billion of reserves defending it, and the Federal Reserve’s own hiking cycle, with another increase expected in December, keeps the interest rate gap wide. That gap leaves the yen prone to further weakness, and one economist warned that skipping a December move could push it lower still and add to imported inflation.

Equity turbulence is not seen as a deal breaker. The Nikkei 225 has fallen about 7% this month, largely on doubts over whether the pace of global AI investment can last, but 83% of respondents to a separate question said the volatility would not stop a December hike. Another economist said a pause remains possible if the AI-driven selloff keeps rattling markets, while still treating a hike as the baseline.

Wages offer the BOJ another reason for confidence. Economists expect next year’s spring labour talks to deliver pay rises of around 5.00%, just below this year’s 5.01%, which would make a fourth straight year of increases at roughly that pace. Forecasts ranged from 4.25% to 5.50%. Sustained wage gains of that size are the kind of evidence the BOJ has long said it needs to keep normalising policy, and they make a December move look like a continuation of a plan rather than a reaction to the yen alone. 

---

item.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83, above range, setting up Thursday’s Nasdaq debut as ANT
item.description:
How ANT trades on debut is likely to shape sentiment across the wider AI complex. Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Amazon and Google are all investors, partners or suppliers, so their shares may react to how ANT opens. Asian chip and memory stocks that supply AI hardware could feel the knock-on effect in Friday’s session. Rates are the main risk to the AI trade. With several Fed officials leaning toward further hikes, any rise in Treasury yields would sharpen worries about funding costs for data centres and neoclouds. A strong debut could ease those worries for now, while a soft one would add to them.

---

Anthropic’s above-range pricing shows the big money is keen, but Thursday’s opening trade will show whether public markets agree, at a time when AI stocks are already uneasy about rates, politics and leadership upheaval.

Summary:

  • Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the $70 to $78 range it set last week
  • Trading is expected to begin on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19, with no scheduled time for the first trade (in case you are wondering)
  • Amazon and Google each hold stakes worth more than $100 billion, and a big tech group agreed to invest $26 billion in the offering
  • Revenue for the nine months to September was around $33 billion, up roughly 1,200%, and run-rate revenue reached about $81 billion in October
  • The nine-month net loss was around $104 billion, mostly from fair-value changes on convertible notes and derivatives
  • The listing comes after recent shocks to the AI sector, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and worries that rising rates will raise funding costs

Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $83 per share, above the $70 to $78 range it set last week, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing a person familiar with the matter. The Claude developer is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, November 19.

There is no scheduled time for the first trade. That is normal for an IPO: a new listing opens only once the exchange and the underwriters have matched enough buy and sell orders to set an opening price, which can take anywhere from minutes to several hours after the regular session begins.

Pricing above the range points to strong institutional demand, and it comes at a sensitive moment for the artificial intelligence trade. The sector has been rattled by a run of shocks, including a voter backlash against AI that showed up in the midterm elections and the ouster of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang last week. Investors were already uneasy that rising interest rates could make debt too expensive for many data centre developers and so-called neoclouds, the specialist providers that rent out AI computing capacity.

The deal also ties together much of big tech. Amazon and Google each hold stakes in Anthropic worth more than $100 billion, and a group including Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to invest a combined $26 billion in the offering. Anthropic, in turn, is a major buyer of computing systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD, so the reception for ANT shares will be read as a verdict on that whole web of spending.

The growth figures help explain the appetite. Anthropic reported revenue of around $33 billion for the nine months to September 30, up roughly 1,200% from a year earlier, driven largely by demand for its Claude Code programming tool. It said its annualised run-rate revenue reached about $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion in a month. The company booked a net loss of around $104 billion over the nine months, although most of that reflected changes in the fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities rather than operating losses.

Investors have plenty to weigh. The prospectus runs to more than 90 pages of risk factors, and the company has had two high-profile disputes with the US government this year over safety, regulation and national security. Competition is also fierce: Anthropic is racing OpenAI and Google for enterprise customers, and OpenAI, which has confidentially filed for its own listing, has said a debut is likely in 2027.

How ANT trades once it opens will show whether public markets share the enthusiasm seen in the book. A strong debut could steady sentiment across AI stocks after a bruising few weeks, while a weak one would feed the doubts about rates, funding costs and stretched valuations that have been building in the sector. 

What is this, a dollar for ANTs?

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Kashkari says markets see more Fed hikes than officials do as four Fed voices turn hawkish
item.description:
Hawkish Fed remarks arriving one after another should support the US dollar and keep front-end Treasury yields firm going into December. Gold is the asset most exposed. Through this cycle it has fallen as Fed hike expectations build, so more tightening talk is a headwind rather than a bid. For the Australian dollar, which is already near 10-month lows, a Fed that keeps hiking narrows the policy gap with the RBA. That raises the stakes for today’s Australian jobs data. If Kashkari is right that the shocks behind inflation are supply-driven, oil remains the key input to watch, because further energy price spikes would strengthen the hawks’ case.

---

When a voting Fed official says markets expect more hikes than his colleagues do and makes no effort to push back, the message is that the policy path may have to rise to meet the pricing.

Summary:

  • Minneapolis Fed President Kashkari said markets believe the Fed will need to hike more than officials currently expect
  • He said elevated inflation has come from a series of supply shocks, and that keeping inflation expectations anchored is essential
  • He described the strength of US demand as somewhat surprising and the job market as resilient
  • He said interest rates can clearly affect investment levels
  • Waller, Daly and Barr also sounded hawkish on Wednesday, with Waller again floating a  (not gonna happen, IMHO ;-) ) 50 basis point hike
  • The Fed held at 3.75% to 4.00% in October, with two dissents in favour of a hike

Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Neel Kashkari said on Wednesday that markets believe the Fed will have to raise interest rates further than officials currently expect, a notable remark from a policymaker who votes on the Federal Open Market Committee this year. He made no attempt, in the comments reported, to talk that pricing down.

Kashkari traced the current bout of elevated inflation to a series of supply shocks and said the Fed’s priority must be keeping inflation expectations anchored. That framing matters. Central bankers often argue they can look through supply shocks, but only if the public keeps faith that inflation will return to target. When shocks arrive one after another, that faith becomes harder to take for granted, and Kashkari’s emphasis on expectations suggests he sees the risk as real rather than theoretical.

He also said the strength of demand has been a little surprising and described the labour market as resilient. Both points weaken the case for patience. A firm economy gives the Fed room to keep tightening without tipping it into a sharp downturn, and a resilient jobs market removes one of the main arguments a more cautious official might make for pausing. Kashkari added that interest rates can absolutely affect investment, pushing back on any suggestion that higher borrowing costs have lost their bite.

His comments landed on a day when several colleagues were sounding a similar note. Governor Christopher Waller, Governor Michael Barr and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly all struck hawkish tones on Wednesday, with Waller once again raising the possibility of a 50 basis point hike. A move of that size remains an outside possibility rather than the base case, but the fact that it is being discussed openly shows how far the debate has shifted toward the scale of further tightening rather than whether it is needed.

The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% at its late October meeting, with two officials dissenting in favour of a quarter point increase. Since then, hotter inflation data and a steady run of hawkish commentary have reinforced expectations of a hike at the December meeting.

Kashkari’s remark on market pricing is the one to watch. If officials begin publicly endorsing a higher path than their own projections imply, the December forecasts could shift up to meet the market, rather than the market moving back toward the Fed.

There are many more than one of these! A "Fed" of hawks!
